stimulus.content:
“Every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. We have called by different names brethren of the same principle. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists. . . . peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none . . .”
—Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address, 1801
stimulus.citation: Thomas Jefferson, First Inaugural Address (March 4, 1801), The Avalon Project, Yale Law School

question: Which reading of the passage is best supported?

options.A: Jefferson claimed that political parties no longer existed in the United States
options.B: Jefferson stressed that disagreement need not mean abandoning shared principles
options.C: Jefferson urged an alliance with European powers to protect trade
options.D: Jefferson asked Americans to adopt the Federalist program as national policy

explanation: Jefferson emphasized that Americans shared fundamental principles despite party differences and rejected “entangling alliances” with foreign nations.

distractor_notes.A: He acknowledged “different names,” so parties still existed.
distractor_notes.C: He rejected “entangling alliances” with any nation.
distractor_notes.D: He did not endorse the Federalist program; he spoke of shared principles.

trap.trap_description: The passage is conciliatory, and the tempting reading takes the line about Federalists as a surrender of Republican principles.
trap.why_students_fall_for_it: The words “we are all Federalists” can be read as endorsing the Federalist program.
trap.how_to_avoid: Read the whole sentence and note the lowercase meaning of “republicans” and “federalists” as shared principles, plus the rejection of “entangling alliances.”
